extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and reporters of wartime news (AP/newspaper audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting battlefield and wartime events for a newspaper/press wire (AP-style dispatches), including datelines, eyewitness detail, official communiqués, and the logistical constraints of transmitting copy during wartime. Emphasis on timeliness, attribution, and vivid scene-setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / perishable news
rubrics_metrics.description: “When an army is on the move news ... becomes cold before you can get it on paper because something is happening or going to happen which is bigger and better news than what you have. By the time the story is finished, it's old--the army is moving on to new gains.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that frontline news is highly perishable; reporters must work quickly and recognize that a dispatch may be out-of-date by publication. The piece explicitly frames battlefield dispatches as rapidly superseded and stresses urgency in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispatch routing and censorship procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: “When this is written a dispatch rider will take it back over more than 200 miles of desert to a landing ground where a plane will fly it to Tripoli. From Tripoli another plane will carry it to Algiers for censorship. To London and by transatlantic cable to New York.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field copy must follow wartime transmission chains (dispatch rider → plane → censorship center → London → transatlantic cable). Reporters should plan for these logistical steps and the resulting delays; also anticipate that after reaching allied hubs copy may be further sent by wireless or cable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use official communiqués as sourcing for operational claims
rubrics_metrics.description: “The weather was clear 'and the target was-heavily and accurately bombed and left on fire,' said a joint communique of the British Air ministry and 8th U. S. Air Force headquarters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on and cite official military communiqués for claims about strikes, damage, and operational outcomes; attribute such statements clearly to the issuing authorities rather than presenting them as independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of reports and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases throughout: “a dispatch from Rome said today,” “reported,” “the broadcast, recorded by the Associated Press,” “recorded here by the federal communications commission.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always attribute assertions and reports to their originating source (dispatches, broadcasts, official agencies). Indicate when information comes from other newspapers, radio broadcasts, or recorded sources to convey provenance and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include eyewitness and human-detail scene-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: “The wrecked village of Sedjenane ... presents a traditional picture of the wreckage, desolation and violence associated with modern warfare. ... you see scattered shell holes and frequent rows or groups of German graves. ... some of the graves are marked by neatly-lettered names on wooden crosses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, concrete details and human-interest elements (village wreckage, graves, personal anecdotes) to convey the reality and emotional impact of war. Scene description and small human details strengthen a dispatch's narrative and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark and explain reporting delays (use of 'DELAYED')
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline markers and parentheticals such as “(DELAYED)” and commentary: “This story is old before my fingers can type the words ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If copy is delayed from the event, label it as such and, where appropriate, explain the reason for delay so readers understand timing and potential staleness of the information.
